content: Preventive chemotherapy is a critical component of a comprehensive strategy to reduce the morbidity caused by soil-transmitted helminths in at-risk populations. However, it is not sufficient on its own to achieve complete elimination of the disease burden. The following points provide detailed guidance for implementing these recommendations: 1. The prevalence and intensity of soil-transmitted helminth infections are closely related. In areas where the baseline prevalence of any soil-transmitted helminth infection is below 20%, only light-intensity infections and low morbidity are expected. In such cases, large-scale preventive chemotherapy programs are not necessary. 2. Administering preventive chemotherapy to adolescent girls and women of reproductive age requires additional caution. It is essential to ensure that women and girls receiving anthelmintic medications are not pregnant. Policymakers may choose to withhold preventive chemotherapy in this population if pregnancy status or gestational age is uncertain, or in regions with high rates of unplanned pregnancies and low antenatal care coverage. 3. Additional resources may be needed to deliver preventive chemotherapy to adolescent girls, as they may not be easily accessible through existing healthcare infrastructure. 4. Anthelmintic medications can be safely administered to individuals co-infected with HIV, provided they meet the eligibility criteria for inclusion in large-scale preventive chemotherapy interventions. 5. Adequate water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services are fundamental to breaking the cycle of infection and reinfection, thereby ensuring sustainable control of soil-transmitted helminth infections. Collaboration between helminth control programs and WASH initiatives is essential to prioritize these services in endemic areas. 6. Deworming interventions should be integrated with health and hygiene promotion to reduce transmission. Encouraging healthy behaviors, such as handwashing, wearing footwear, and proper disposal of feces, is critical. 7. Routine monitoring of coverage and evaluation of the impact of preventive chemotherapy programs should be an integral part of these interventions. This will help inform decisions on whether to continue or discontinue the program. 8. Research gaps have been identified in several areas, including: Diagnostic or proxy indicators to identify households at risk and individuals infected with soil-transmitted helminths. Alternative anthelmintic medications or combinations in case of drug resistance to albendazole or mebendazole. Estimation of species-specific infection intensities that cause morbidity related to nutrient absorption, utilization, and growth. Innovative distribution systems to reach vulnerable groups, such as adolescent girls, with considerations for equity. The effects of combining anthelmintic medications with other nutritional, environmental, WASH, or hygiene interventions on nutritional outcomes and reinfection rates. Active identification and documentation of adverse effects in specific populations, such as individuals living with HIV (especially children and those on antiretroviral therapy), breastfeeding mothers and their infants, pregnant women and their unborn babies, and infants under 12 months of age. Factors influencing compliance with large-scale preventive chemotherapy programs, including the values and preferences of children, adolescent girls, and adult women, as well as prevailing social attitudes toward treatment of soil-transmitted helminth infections and the role of health education in improving compliance rates. 9. The World Health Organization (WHO) will continue to monitor research developments in preventive chemotherapy for at-risk populations, particularly in areas where the quality of evidence is currently low or very low. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, WHO will conduct a search for new evidence to update the recommendations as needed. 10. Soil-transmitted helminth infections are caused by nematodes such as Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), and hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus). These infections are among the most common in humans, particularly affecting those living in poverty. In endemic areas with inadequate sanitation, parasite eggs are excreted in the feces of infected individuals, contaminating the soil. Humans become infected by ingesting eggs or larvae or through skin penetration by hookworm larvae. Reinfection occurs through contact with infectious stages in the environment, as these worms do not multiply within the human host. 11. Globally, nearly 2 billion people (approximately one-quarter of the world’s population) are infected with soil-transmitted helminths. This includes around 270 million preschool children, over 550 million school-age children, and approximately 250 million girls and adult women living in endemic areas. The highest burden is observed in sub-Saharan Africa, the Americas, and Asia, with more than 100 countries affected. 12. Preventive chemotherapy aims to reduce the worm burden in children, adolescent girls, women of reproductive age, and pregnant women, including those co-infected with HIV. The guideline provides evidence-based recommendations to inform discussions among stakeholders when selecting or prioritizing interventions in specific contexts. It also emphasizes the importance of integrating deworming efforts with broader public health strategies, such as improving nutrition and ensuring access to safe and hygienic environments.
